items.prompt: Define a market schedule for demand and supply.
items.canonical_answer: A record of quantities demanded and supplied at stated prices over a stated period.
marking_guidance: Definition: price-quantity record, 1; qualifier: planned buying/selling over a period, 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Use these data to draw original demand and supply curves: price N$8, N$12, N$16; weekly demand 80,60,40 units; weekly supply 40,60,80. Put quantity on the horizontal axis and price on the vertical axis. Show the change along both curves when price rises from N$8 to N$16 (4).
items.canonical_answer: Plot D through (80,8),(60,12),(40,16) and S through (40,8),(60,12),(80,16). Label price N$ per unit vertically and units per week horizontally. D slopes down, S up; arrows run up-left on D and up-right on S for the stated price rise.
marking_guidance: Diagram: axes/labels 1, original D points/line 1, original S points/line 1, change arrows along existing curves 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain the relationship in a market schedule where price rises from N$6 to N$9, quantity demanded falls from 70 to 50 and quantity supplied rises from 30 to 50 units per week, other conditions unchanged.
items.canonical_answer: Demand has a negative price relationship while supply has a positive one. Buyers plan 20 fewer units and producers 20 more. The changes are movements along existing curves because the product’s own price changes with other conditions fixed. At N$9 both planned quantities are 50.
marking_guidance: Relationship: opposite demand/supply directions 1; evidence: stated quantities 1; explanation: own-price movements, not shifts 2.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain why a lower price of a snack causing more purchases, with income and tastes unchanged, is not a demand-curve shift.
items.canonical_answer: The snack’s own price changed (1), so the greater quantity is a movement along the existing demand curve (1).
marking_guidance: Context: snack; reasoning: own-price change 1; result: movement rather than shift 1.

items.prompt: Define equilibrium price.
items.canonical_answer: The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied over the stated period.
marking_guidance: Meaning: market price 1; distinguishing feature: equality of planned quantities 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Use a diagram to show equilibrium for weekly demand points (quantity, price): (90,10),(60,20),(30,30), and supply points (30,10),(60,20),(90,30). Prices are N$ per packet. Mark the change towards equilibrium from N$10 (4).
items.canonical_answer: Draw labelled D and S on quantity-per-week and N$-price axes. The original intersection E is (60,20); project N$20 and 60 onto the axes. At N$10 mark Qs 30 and Qd 90, excess demand 60; show upward price adjustment towards N$20.
marking_guidance: Diagram labels/axes 1; original curves 1; E and projections 1; change from shortage with upward adjustment 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain what happens at a price of N$30 when demand is 30 and supply is 90 packets per week, while at N$20 both are 60. Assume price can adjust.
items.canonical_answer: At N$30 there is excess supply of 60 packets per week. Sellers face offers greater than planned purchases, putting downward pressure on price. As it falls along unchanged curves, demand quantity rises and supply quantity falls. N$20 is equilibrium because both quantities equal 60 there.
marking_guidance: Relationship: excess supply 1; evidence: 90 minus 30 equals 60, with equilibrium equality 1; explanation: downward adjustment and movements 2.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain why 100 units offered and 65 units wanted at a price of N$40 do not show equilibrium.
items.canonical_answer: Supply exceeds demand by 35 units (1), so the planned quantities are unequal rather than in equilibrium (1).
marking_guidance: Context: offers versus wants; reasoning: excess supply 1; result: not equilibrium 1.

items.prompt: Explain the error in showing a price ceiling alone as a leftward shift of demand.
items.canonical_answer: The control specifies a permitted price rather than changing quantities buyers want at each price (1), so it is shown as a horizontal price level against the existing curves (1).
marking_guidance: Confusion: price rule versus curve determinant; boundary/test: permitted price line versus changed relationship, 1 each.

items.prompt: Define an increase in demand.
items.canonical_answer: An increase in quantities buyers are willing and able to buy at each price, shown by a rightward demand shift.
marking_guidance: Definition: more at each price 1; qualifier: demand relationship shifts right 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Use a diagram for seed packets to show an increase in demand. Original weekly demand at N$10,20,30 is 90,60,30; new demand is 120,90,60; unchanged supply is 30,60,90. Use straight lines and label both equilibria (4).
items.canonical_answer: Plot D0 through (90,10),(60,20),(30,30); D1 through (120,10),(90,20),(60,30); S through (30,10),(60,20),(90,30). Label E0=(60,20), E1=(75,25), and projections. D1 is right of D0; price rises N$20 to N$25 and quantity 60 to 75.
marking_guidance: Diagram labels/axes 1; original D0/S 1; demand change D1 rightward 1; equilibria/projections 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain the effect of an increase in supply where the old equilibrium is N$20 and 60 packets weekly, and the new equilibrium is N$15 and 75 with demand unchanged.
items.canonical_answer: The supply curve shifts right, meaning more offered at given prices. At the old price the extra offers create excess supply, pushing price down. The new equilibrium price is N$5 lower and quantity 15 packets higher; buyers move along unchanged demand.
marking_guidance: Relationship: supply rightward 1; evidence: price/quantity changes 1; explanation: excess supply and movement along demand 2.

items.prompt: Explain the likely market effect of improved production technology for a cup maker when demand is unchanged.
items.canonical_answer: Lower production difficulty or cost allows more cups to be offered at each price (1), so supply shifts right, tending to lower equilibrium price and raise quantity (1).
marking_guidance: Context: cup production; reasoning: more at each price 1; result: supply increase effects 1.

items.prompt: Define a non-price determinant of demand or supply.
items.canonical_answer: A factor other than the product’s own price that changes quantities demanded or supplied at given prices.

items.prompt: Explain how higher cloth costs can affect the supply of shirts.
items.canonical_answer: Initial change: cloth costs rise (1); producing shirts becomes more costly for the firm, reducing the amount it is willing to offer at each price (1).

items.canonical_answer: Tea becomes relatively more expensive (1), so some buyers may switch to the herbal drink, raising its demand at given prices (1).

items.prompt: Explain the error in treating a rise in household income as an increase in producers’ supply merely because households buy more.
items.canonical_answer: The change directly affects buyers’ willingness and ability to purchase (1), so for a normal good it shifts demand; higher production following a price response is not itself proof of a supply shift (1).
marking_guidance: Confusion: buyer versus producer determinant; boundary/test: quantities at given prices, 1 each.

items.prompt: Explain why a brand of maize meal and maize meal as a whole are not a clear pair of substitutes.
items.canonical_answer: The brand belongs inside the product category (1); a substitute pair needs distinct alternatives, such as maize meal and another staple used instead (1).
marking_guidance: Confusion: member/category mistaken for alternatives; boundary/test: two separate replacement choices, 1 each.

items.prompt: Explain why greater demand after a change in tastes is not, by itself, evidence of greater price elasticity.
items.canonical_answer: Tastes can change quantities wanted at given prices, shifting demand (1); elasticity concerns quantity responsiveness to the product’s own price, which this fact does not measure (1).
marking_guidance: Confusion: shift versus responsiveness; boundary/test: given-price change versus own-price response, 1 each.

items.prompt: Define excess demand.
items.canonical_answer: The amount by which quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at a stated price.
marking_guidance: Definition: demand quantity greater than supply 1; qualifier: difference at stated price 1.

items.prompt: Use a diagram to show a supply increase with unchanged weekly demand. At N$10,20,30 demand is 90,60,30; original supply is 30,60,90 and new supply 60,90,120. Label the original and changed equilibria (4).
items.canonical_answer: Draw D unchanged; S0 through (30,10),(60,20),(90,30); S1 through (60,10),(90,20),(120,30). The supply change is rightward. E0=(60,20); E1=(75,15). Show N$20 falling to N$15 and weekly quantity 60 rising to 75 using projections.
marking_guidance: Diagram axes/labels 1; original D/S0 1; change S1 rightward 1; equilibria and projections 1.

items.prompt: Explain why a market experiencing both higher demand and higher supply cannot be assigned a definite new price without more information.
items.canonical_answer: Higher demand tends to push price up; higher supply tends to push it down. The opposing influences mean their relative size determines the net price effect. For example, a large demand increase with a small supply increase can raise price, while the reverse can lower it.
marking_guidance: Relationship: opposing price pressures 1; evidence: explicit contrasting relative-shift examples 1; explanation: net effect requires magnitude information 2.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain the effect of a crop failure reducing vegetable supply when demand is unchanged.
items.canonical_answer: Less is offered at each price (1), so the supply reduction tends to raise equilibrium price and lower equilibrium quantity (1).
marking_guidance: Context: crop failure; reasoning: leftward supply change 1; result: price up/quantity down 1.

items.prompt: At the Sandridge seed market, weekly prices N$10,20,30 correspond to demand of 90,60,30 packets and supply of 30,60,90. A gardening campaign increases demand to 120,90,60 at those prices, with supply unchanged. Assume straight lines and flexible prices. (a) Describe three features of the schedules (6). (b) Examine the effect of the campaign on equilibrium (7). (c) Suggest how traders should interpret the higher price before planning stock (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Demand falls by 30 packets for each N$10 price increase. Supply rises by 30. Original equilibrium is N$20 and 60 packets because plans are equal. (b) Demand shifts right by 30 packets at each price. At N$20 there is excess demand of 30, creating upward price pressure. The new intersection is N$25 and 75 packets weekly. Supply has not shifted: producers move along it as price rises. (c) Traders should treat the change as evidence of higher demand, not lower supply. Planning may allow for 75 rather than 60 packets under the stated model, but an individual trader should not assume it supplies the whole market. Check whether the campaign effect persists and whether its own capacity fits the extra sales. A temporary campaign or other changing conditions could make the estimated new equilibrium short-lived; the judgement depends on continuing demand and unchanged supply conditions.
marking_guidance: Context: Sandridge. Parts/allocation: (a) demand pattern 2, supply pattern 2, equality 2 = 6. (b) shift 2, excess-demand mechanism 2, new equilibrium 2, movement along S 1 = 7. (c) correct interpretation 2, market-versus-firm distinction 2, conditional stock judgement and persistence 3 = 7.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: (a) Define equilibrium price (2). (b) Explain why an own-price change need not shift demand (2). (c) Explain one demand determinant unrelated to own price (2). (d) Explain one supply determinant unrelated to own price (2). (e) Explain why a brand and its containing product category are not a distinct substitute pair (2). (f) Explain what excess supply means (2). (g) Explain why imposing a price level alone does not move the curves (2). (h) Explain why simultaneous demand and supply increases leave the net price direction uncertain without magnitudes (2).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Price where quantities demanded and supplied are equal. (b) It changes quantity along the existing relationship, other conditions fixed. (c) Higher income can raise demand for a normal good by supporting purchases at given prices. (d) Lower input costs can increase planned offers at given prices. (e) One is contained in the other rather than being a distinct replacement product. (f) Supply quantity exceeds demand quantity at the stated price, leaving excess offers. (g) A rule about price does not itself change buyers’ or sellers’ quantities at every given price. (h) The shifts push price in opposite directions, so relative size matters.
marking_guidance: Parts/allocation and precision: eight 2-mark parts. (a) price + quantity equality; (b) own price + movement; (c) buyer factor + given-price effect; (d) producer factor + given-price effect; (e) category membership + missing distinct alternatives; (f) excess quantity + stated price; (g) rule/relationship distinction; (h) opposing influences + relative magnitudes.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: At a vegetable market, bad weather reduces quantities growers can supply at each price. Buyers’ incomes and preferences are unchanged. Initially price was N$12 per bundle and equilibrium quantity 200 bundles weekly. No new schedule or size of the supply reduction is supplied. (a) Define supply (2). (b) Explain two distinctions needed to analyse the event (4). (c) Explain the effect on the market using a labelled demand-and-supply diagram (7). (d) Discuss whether a trader can conclude that total weekly sales receipts must rise (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Quantities producers are willing and able to offer at different prices over a period, other conditions unchanged. (b) Weather changes quantities at given prices, shifting supply rather than causing an own-price movement. Buyers’ conditions are unchanged, so demand stays in place even though quantity demanded changes with price. (c) Draw downward D and upward S0, label E0 and initial price N$12/quantity 200. Shift S left to S1. At the old price demand exceeds the reduced offer, tending to raise price. E1 has higher price and lower quantity; label projections but do not invent figures. (d) Each bundle sells at a higher price, tending to raise receipts per unit, but fewer bundles are sold, tending to reduce receipts. Without the size of each change, total price-times-quantity receipts cannot be established. A trader also needs its own quantity rather than treating the market as its business. The defensible judgement is that total receipts are uncertain, even though the direction of market price is clear.
marking_guidance: Context: vegetable market. Parts/allocation: (a) producer willingness/ability 1, price/period qualifier 1. (b) two distinctions, each contrast + reason 2 = 4. (c) diagram labels/original 2, leftward change 1, shortage mechanism 2, new P/Q directions 2 = 7. (d) higher-price influence 2, lower-quantity influence 2, judgement avoiding unsupported magnitude and market/firm inference 3 = 7.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether a higher observed price is enough evidence for a local food supplier to conclude demand has increased, when no information on quantities or production conditions is supplied (9).
items.canonical_answer: For: higher demand with unchanged supply would raise equilibrium price, so the observation is consistent with a demand increase. Against: a supply reduction with unchanged demand would also raise price but reduce quantity. Both sides may change, and relative shifts matter. A price observation alone cannot identify which determinant moved or establish the quantity effect. Judgement: obtain evidence about quantities, buyer circumstances and producer costs before assigning the cause. The condition for the simple demand explanation is credible evidence that supply conditions were unchanged and buyers wanted more at given prices. The higher price alone does not meet that condition.
marking_guidance: Argument for: demand-shift mechanism with unchanged supply, up to 4. Argument against: alternative supply mechanism and simultaneous changes, up to 4. Judgement: distinct evidence condition, 1. Total 9.
